claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is an appropriate single-phase FCC baseline alloy.
The CoCrFeMnNi baseline has relatively high density and limited weight savings.
Adding lighter elements such as Al or Ti will lower the alloy's overall density.
Al or Ti substitution in a multi-principal-element alloy will promote a light-element-enriched matrix and secondary nanoscale features.
A dual-scale microstructure can mediate the simultaneous achievement of low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
A light-element-enriched matrix will form an adherent, stable protective oxide during high-temperature exposure.
The protective oxide will be viscous and self-healing, with behavior similar to CrTaO4- or Al2O3-based scales.
Deformation-induced nanoscale twins can provide sustained strain hardening and damage tolerance.
Finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates will provide strain hardening in the proposed lightweight alloy.
Controlled polymorphic transitions will drive the formation or dispersion of the nanoscale strengthening features.
Oxidation will cause preferential chemical redistribution governed by thermodynamic and redox tendencies.
The lightweight variant will have 10–20% lower density than the CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
The lightweight variant will retain or moderately improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline.
The lightweight variant will exhibit superior corrosion resistance, including lower passive current densities, in chloride- or fluoride-containing media.
The lightweight variant will show lower oxidation weight gain than the CoCrFeMnNi baseline during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Loss of oxide-scale adherence or rapid oxide degradation above a critical temperature will eliminate the proposed oxidation-protection mechanism.
Coarsening of nanoscale reinforcements during prolonged service will reduce strain hardening.
Light-element additions may impair passivation in sufficiently aggressive environments, causing the proposed corrosion benefit to fail.
